title: Whipped Tallow Balm in Pear: What My Skin Did When I Tried Beef Fat
body:
Okay so I put beef fat on my face. I know. It sounds like something you’d do on a dare, or maybe in a weird, desperate moment when you’ve run out of everything else. That was basically me, back in like, February. My skin was just… done. It was that gross spring where it’s not cold but it’s not warm, just windy and mean, and my face felt like old paper. Tight. Flaky in weird spots. I’d tried the fancy stuff, the stuff in the heavy glass jars that costs more than my electric bill. Made things shiny. Didn’t fix the tight.

Anyway. I was scrolling, probably avoiding work, and I saw this thing about tallow balm. Beef tallow skincare. Specifically this whipped one that said it was pear scented. My brain did the thing. Beef. Pear. Face. Those words do not belong together. But I was curious enough to click. And then I was curious enough, and annoyed enough with my skin, to actually get some. From this little Etsy shop. It arrived in a normal box. I opened it thinking this was either genius or a huge mistake.

## How I Started Putting Beef Tallow on My Face

Let’s rewind. My initial reaction was pure skepticism. You’re telling me to smear rendered cow fat on the same skin I’m trying to keep clear? It felt backwards. Like using gasoline to put out a fire. I grew up with Noxzema and Clean & Clear. This was not in the brochure.

But then I started poking around. And I got distracted, because I always do—I fell into a rabbit hole about my grandma. She didn’t call it tallow skincare. She had this little tin of something she’d put on her hands in winter. It was solid, waxy. She said it was “just the good stuff.” I never asked what “the good stuff” was. Probably lard. Or yeah, tallow. People used what they had. For centuries, apparently. It wasn’t a fancy trend, it was just… what worked. Before labs and chemical names and twenty-step routines. That got me thinking.

The science-y bit, which I will butcher because I’m not a scientist, is that the fat from grass-fed cows—the suet—is structurally really close to the oils our own skin makes. Our sebum. So when you put this tallow balm on, your skin kinda recognizes it. It doesn’t just sit on top like a greasy film from some lotions. It’s like it gets an invitation to come in. It absorbs. It’s a compatible molecule thing. I’m probably explaining this terribly. The point is, it makes biological sense, even if the idea of rubbing steak juice on your cheek sounds insane.

So I opened the jar. The texture was weird. Not bad weird. It’s whipped, so it’s like this super dense, creamy cloud. You scoop a tiny bit and it melts the second it hits your finger. Cold at first. Then it just becomes oil. I held it up to my nose. Pear? Yeah, sort of. But not like a Jolly Rancher. More like if you walked past a pear tree on a cool morning. A fresh, light sweetness. Nothing overpowering. Nothing fake. It just smelled clean and a little fruity. Gentle. I was relieved it didn’t smell like a barn.

## Why This Tallow Balm Actually Does Something

I started using it at night. After I washed my face, I’d take a dab about the size of a pea. Rub it between my palms to warm it up and then just press it all over. My first thought was that I’d wake up a greaseball.

I did not.

Here’s the thing. It sinks in. It doesn’t vanish, but that heavy, tight feeling on my face was just… gone. In the morning, my skin didn’t feel parched. It felt quiet. Normal. Not screaming for moisture. I kept using it. My dry patches—gone in like, three days. The little line I get between my eyebrows when I’m stressed looked less like a canyon. I started using it on my hands too, because why not. I type all day and they get gross. The balm fixed the cracking around my knuckles faster than the thick “healing” cream I’d been using for months.

The benefits of this tallow stuff, for me, were super straightforward. It’s deeply hydrating because it mimics my skin’s own stuff. It’s just grass-fed beef tallow and some essential oils for scent. That’s it. No mile-long ingredient list I can’t pronounce. It fixed winter damage. My lips stopped chapping. I even dab a bit on my elbows, which are always rough. They’re actually smooth now. It’s wild.

I got sidetracked just now. My neighbor started mowing his lawn. At 8 PM. Who does that? Anyway.

## My Skin Now (And Where I Got The Stuff)

So it’s been a few weeks. Maybe a month? I’ve lost track. I’m still using it. I’m probably halfway through the jar. My skin just feels… balanced. It’s not a miracle. I didn’t turn into a dewy newborn. But the constant dryness battle is over. I don’t think about my skin anymore, which is the highest compliment I can give. It just does its thing.

I mentioned I got it on Etsy. The shop is called Pure Sway. I’m not getting anything for saying this, I just like what they made. It feels like someone took care making it. The balm is whipped in France, which is a detail I appreciate for no good reason. It feels fancy but in a simple way. I like supporting the small makers doing this kind of stuff. Feels less weird than buying beef tallow skincare from a giant corporation, you know?

Would I buy it again? Yeah. I already am. I’m getting another jar for my mom. She has that thin, delicate skin that gets irritated by everything. I think this will just… work for her. Like it did for her mom, probably, even if she didn’t know it.

## Quick Questions I Get Asked

**Is beef tallow good for your face?**
Weirdly, yes. Because it’s so similar to the oils our skin already produces, it absorbs well and helps reinforce your skin’s own barrier. It’s not just sitting on top clogging things up. It’s like giving your skin something it actually knows how to use.

**Does tallow balm clog pores?**
From everything I’ve read and from my own experience, no. Because it’s so compatible, it sinks in instead of forming a pore-clogging layer. My skin is pretty normal but can get congested easily, and this hasn’t caused any issues. It’s the opposite—my skin seems calmer.

**What does the Pear tallow balm smell like?**
It’s light. It’s not a candy pear. It’s more like the idea of a fresh pear, with a clean, subtle sweetness. It’s not strong at all. It fades pretty quickly after you put it on, which I like. You’re not walking around smelling like fruit salad.

So yeah. That’s my beef fat story. It just works. I don’t have a better way to say it. If your skin is being difficult, feeling tight or dry or just off, it might be worth a shot. It’s one of those simple things that shouldn’t work but somehow does. My elbows haven’t been this smooth since… I don’t know when.
